201: Structured pruning removes less useful CNN filters, reducing inference computation; captured training tensors can inform which filters to prune.
Ordinary CloudWatch algorithm metrics do not expose the detailed weight, gradient, and activation tensors needed for the proposed filter analysis.
Debugger supplies useful tensors, but generic hyperparameter adjustment does not explicitly reduce the convolutional computation that drives inference latency.

Debugger can provide tensors for ranking filters. Removing low-value filters and retraining the smaller network can reduce inference work while recovering accuracy; latency must be benchmarked on the target hardware.
ModelLatency and OverheadLatency are endpoint performance metrics in CloudWatch. Model Monitor focuses on data and prediction-quality issues, and the option omits a concrete compression method.
202: TensorFlow script mode runs a user training script with managed training infrastructure and supports training channels backed by S3 without converting TFRecord files.
TensorFlow can consume TFRecord data directly. An extra format-conversion pipeline and second bucket add work without addressing a requirement.
Rewriting the script for an unnecessary conversion increases development effort. A local path alone also does not provide a scalable remote training data source.
Keeping TFRecord is appropriate, but pointing a remote training job at a notebook-local path does not make that local data available to its training instances.
S3-backed input channels supply the existing TFRecord dataset to the managed TensorFlow job. The script must already read the configured training-channel path for it to run unchanged.
203: Managed Spot Training reduces compute cost, while periodically saved checkpoints let interrupted training resume from saved state.
Batch can run Spot jobs, but the described job lacks checkpoint and resume handling. Retrying an interrupted job can repeat work from the beginning.
Self-managed Spot instances require custom orchestration and interruption handling. Relying only on the short interruption notice is less robust than regularly saving checkpoints.
Lambda has limited execution duration and no GPU instances. It is not suited to long-running training of this large image classifier.
SageMaker manages Spot capacity and checkpoint synchronization. A checkpoint-aware training script can resume after interruption, preserving saved progress while reducing instance cost.
204: Data quality monitoring compares input feature statistics and distributions with a baseline; model quality monitoring evaluates prediction performance against ground truth.
A data quality baseline captures expected feature behavior. A monitoring schedule can compare new data with that baseline, emit violation metrics, and trigger a CloudWatch alarm.
Model quality monitoring can detect degraded forecast accuracy, but the specified change is in input feature distributions, which data quality monitoring targets directly.
Debugger inspects training behavior and tensors. It is not the managed production-data drift comparison needed for these daily forecast inputs.
Standard endpoint metrics describe operational behavior. Detecting feature-distribution drift from logs requires custom calculations that Model Monitor already provides.
205: A SageMaker tuning job can evaluate multiple training definitions using a comparable objective metric, including custom and built-in algorithms.
A custom local-mode search adds orchestration and limits managed parallel tuning. It duplicates capabilities available in automatic model tuning.
Autopilot does not serve as a general hyperparameter tuner for an arbitrary custom image-classification container. Automatic model tuning supports that container directly.
Experiments tracks and organizes runs, but does not itself replace the search strategy and job orchestration of automatic model tuning.
Supplying a training definition for each algorithm lets one managed tuning workflow compare both approaches. They must report equivalent objective metrics on a consistent validation setup.
206: Push selective queries to Redshift and export only the required subset, using managed credential storage or an integrated data-preparation tool.
A distributed Processing cluster adds compute and orchestration for an extraction that Redshift can perform directly. Plotting does not require provisioning that extra cluster.
A manually assembled distributed notebook environment adds management and moves data before filtering it, increasing cost and data movement.
Secrets Manager avoids embedding credentials in the notebook. The client can submit selective SQL and an authorized export, such as UNLOAD, without downloading all 10 TB locally.
Provisioning more than 10 TB of notebook storage and downloading the whole source is unnecessary when only a subset is relevant.
Data Wrangler's Redshift integration provides a managed interface for selecting, inspecting, and exporting relevant data, reducing custom extraction code.
207: BERT sequence classification usually initializes the encoder from pretrained weights and adds a task-specific classifier over the first token representation. The option wording leaves the treatment of the existing head ambiguous.
Preserving pretrained layers except a task head can be appropriate, but this wording does not specify which final layer is meant or how the BERT sequence representation reaches the classifier.

A classifier over the first output position describes the usual CLS-token approach. Full fine-tuning normally updates encoder weights as well, so training only the classifier is not a complete description of that process.
Randomly initializing every layer discards the knowledge learned from Wikipedia and defeats the stated transfer-learning goal.
Replacing a pretrained task-specific head while retaining the encoder is also a legitimate interpretation. The missing distinction between encoder and head prevents an unambiguous single answer.
208: Contact-center analytics depends on both feature support and audio integration. Transcribe Call Analytics and Contact Lens can overlap, so unspecified legacy-platform integration prevents a definitive answer.

Transcribe Call Analytics can provide transcription, categories, and issue-related analytics. If that is what Transcribe means here, the option is plausible, though adding Comprehend may duplicate built-in sentiment features.
Standard transcription plus Comprehend provides useful building blocks, but custom call categorization and issue extraction can require more configuration or model training.

Contact Lens offers the requested contact-center analytics with little custom modeling. Its suitability depends on connecting the legacy telephony audio through a supported integration such as SIPREC.
Contact Lens already includes relevant analytics, so a separate Comprehend stage can add integration work. This option also leaves the same legacy-audio connectivity question unresolved.
209: Forecast validation must mimic predicting future observations from past data, preserving chronological order across the split.
Training on the earliest 80% and validating on the latest 20% evaluates performance on unseen future periods without training on later prices.
Training on later observations and validating on earlier ones reverses the real forecasting direction and can leak information from the future.
Interleaving training and validation points across the series allows later training observations to inform predictions for earlier validation dates.
A random split mixes past and future observations. It can produce overly optimistic results when prices and market conditions are temporally dependent.
210: Personalize user-personalization recipes generate candidate recommendations from interaction history; ranking recipes reorder a candidate list supplied by the caller.
A custom collaborative-filtering model can work, but requires model development, hosting, API integration, and purchase-filtering code.
Personalized Ranking expects an input list of candidate items. The question asks to generate recommendations from user history, so candidate generation would require another step.
User-Personalization with GetRecommendations generates items for each user. A purchase-event filter can exclude previously purchased items within the managed recommendation workflow.
A GPU-trained custom recommender adds training and deployment work without a stated requirement that exceeds Personalize's managed capabilities.
211: Warm-start hyperparameter tuning uses completed tuning results to inform a subsequent search instead of starting without prior observations.
Continuing model training is different from reusing the hyperparameter search. More training iterations alone may not improve the validation accuracy or find a better configuration.
Changing the objective to AUC optimizes ranking across thresholds rather than the requested accuracy. Starting a fresh search also discards the direct warm-start opportunity.

A warm-start tuning job can exploit the existing search history while retaining the comparable validation-accuracy objective. It is the fastest reuse strategy offered, though improvement is not guaranteed.
A new F1 objective and twice as many trials increase the search work and change the optimization target. Neither directly meets the one-day accuracy-improvement constraint.
212: A Glue ETL job transforms and writes data formats at scale; a crawler discovers schemas and updates catalog metadata.
A crawler identifies the CSV schema but does not rewrite CSV objects as Parquet files.
A Glue job can read the CSV dataset and write Parquet using managed distributed processing, avoiding cluster administration for the 20 TB conversion.
An EMR Spark job can perform the conversion, but provisioning and operating the cluster adds work compared with a managed Glue job.
A notebook is an interactive development environment. Converting 20 TB there requires additional resource and job-management work rather than using managed distributed ETL.
213: Kinesis Data Streams provides durable stream ingestion, while Firehose buffers, optionally transforms, and delivers records to destinations such as S3.
The stream supports scalable ingestion and retention. Firehose can consume it, invoke a Lambda transformation, and deliver to S3 within a suitably configured buffering interval.
Writing to S3, moving through a stream, and then returning to S3 adds an unnecessary round trip and event-processing stages.
Starting Glue processing from individual S3 arrivals adds batch orchestration and startup overhead. It is less direct for simple continuous ingestion transformations.
A Firehose delivery stream is not a Glue streaming source in the manner described. Firehose's supported Lambda transformation supplies the required basic processing.
214: Firehose can invoke a Lambda function on incoming batches to transform records before delivering them to S3.
Adding the transformation to the existing delivery stream creates the derived attributes during ingestion without changing software in 20,000 stores or adding a cluster.
A daily EMR cluster adds scheduling, cluster lifecycle management, and a second pass over S3 data for a transformation that fits in the ingestion path.
Installing gateways and changing every store's upload process adds substantial deployment work and does not simplify the existing Firehose pipeline.
An EC2 fleet requires patching, capacity management, scheduling, and failure handling. Managed Firehose transformation avoids those responsibilities.
215: Custom language models use domain text to improve contextual speech recognition; translation converts the resulting English text to the broadcast language.
Custom vocabularies help recognize particular words and names, but do not learn domain usage and context from training and tuning text as custom language models do.
A custom language model can learn sports terminology in context from supplied text. The selected English locale and streaming feature combination must support that model.
Training and hosting a Seq2Seq model introduces model-development work for capabilities available through managed transcription and translation services.
A custom Speech2Text deployment requires selecting, tuning, and operating the model. It has more overhead than the supported Transcribe language-model workflow.
Translate converts the English transcript into French or Spanish. It complements speech recognition; it does not itself transcribe the live audio.
216: Forecast DeepAR+ learned patterns across related time series and could incorporate holiday features. Amazon Forecast is unavailable to new customers, so this is a historical service-selection question.
ARIMA models individual series and does not exploit the collection of related product series in the same global-learning manner as DeepAR+.
DeepAR+ combines learning across related products with managed holiday featurization, meeting the stated requirements with less custom preparation in the historical Forecast workflow.
SageMaker DeepAR can model related series, but the team must build and operate the holiday-enrichment and training pipeline itself.
GluonTS provides forecasting tools, but requires choosing and configuring a model and implementing feature preparation instead of using Forecast's managed feature workflow.
217: With only 1% failure events, class imbalance can hide poor failure detection. Resampling must affect training data only and respect meaningful feature and machine-type boundaries.
The imbalance is between failure and non-failure outcomes, not necessarily among machine types. Weighting machine types does not directly correct that target-class imbalance.

SMOTE creates synthetic minority-class training examples rather than discarding normal observations. With very few failures per machine type, neighbor selection needs care, and improvement must be judged with failure-sensitive metrics.
Undersampling can address imbalance, but discards many normal examples from an already modest dataset. The intended approach preserves those examples while augmenting failures.
SMOTE is an oversampling technique for the minority class. It does not perform the proposed undersampling of non-failure records.
218: Topic modeling discovers latent themes in unlabeled documents; business category names can then be assigned by interpreting those themes.
A custom containerized clustering model requires implementation and maintenance that the built-in topic-modeling algorithm avoids.
K-means can cluster vectorized text, but requires more explicit representation and clustering choices. NTM directly models document topics from suitable text features.

NTM learns topics without predefined category labels, making it appropriate for discovering product-related groups. The topics still need interpretation rather than being guaranteed business categories.
BlazingText supports word embeddings and supervised text classification. Its classification mode requires labels, which the company does not yet have.
219: Rekognition text detection extracts text from natural images without training a custom OCR model.
DetectText can identify the printed race IDs in runner images using a managed API. Image quality and text visibility should be tested on representative race photos.
A custom CNN requires labeled examples, training, and inference operations. Those steps add overhead for a task supported by an existing text-detection API.
Object Detection locates and classifies objects. It does not directly recognize arbitrary character sequences printed on the detected shirts.
Lookout for Vision targeted visual anomalies in industrial inspection, not general text recognition in sports photographs.
220: Batch Transform runs offline inference over S3 datasets and releases its job resources when the batch completes.
The hourly files can be scored in a short batch job without maintaining an endpoint during the long idle interval, matching this periodic offline workload.
Asynchronous Inference supports queued requests and can scale down, but adds endpoint and queue configuration for a task that naturally processes a complete hourly batch.
Processing can run custom inference code, but requires implementing the scoring workflow that Batch Transform provides for the trained model.
A multi-container endpoint is designed for hosted inference and multiple containers. Keeping endpoint capacity for this five-minute hourly batch adds unnecessary cost.
